summary.text:
The paper openly discloses that Lambeth has submitted an application for £116m of exceptional financial support (paragraph 4.19). It sits on top of one of the larger PWLB books we hold: £1,137.7m of external borrowing at a weighted 4.21% at 31 March 2026 (Table 3), of which £1,122.7m is PWLB. Our own file reconciles nearly exactly — 42 PWLB loans totalling £1,112.7m at a weighted 4.17%, £10m and 4bp apart.

The refinancing profile is the interesting part. Table 8 shows a £240.3m new-borrowing requirement in 2026-27 (£193.4m of loans maturing plus £46.9m of CFR growth) against a maturity table (Table 6) where 12.27% sits inside 12 months and 30.5% inside five years. At the far end, 40.48% of the book sits in the 40-50 year bucket — an unusually long-dated portfolio.

The advisor forecast at Table 1 is dated 22 December 2025 and has been overtaken. MUFG's central bet is Bank Rate at 3.25% by the end of 2026-27 (para 3.4), with the 5-year PWLB at 4.30% by September 2026 and the 50-year at 5.40%. Today the 5-year certainty rate is 5.34% (a full point above the September forecast), the 50-year is 6.27%, and the 1-year OIS prices Bank Rate at 4.11% — above the current 3.75% rather than below. MUFG's contract runs to May 2026 and a re-tender is in progress (para 6.2).

Elsewhere: the General Fund financing-cost ratio climbs 2.58pp to 12.95% by 2028-29 while the HRA stays flat around 10.6-11.0% (Table 12); an MRP policy review is flagged for 2026 (para 4.31); Homes for Lambeth exposure sits at £36.7m after Kerslake-driven impairments against an original £150m limit, with a four-company review expected late spring/early summer 2026 (para 6.13).

officer.subject: Your Table 3 ties to our file, and where MUFG's December forecast sits today
officer.body:
Hi,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. Below are a few thoughts on your Treasury Management Strategy for 2026-27, ahead of the mid-year update to Corporate Committee later this year. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your strategy is one of the more candid we've read: paragraph 4.19 flagging the £116m EFS application on the face of the borrowing strategy is a paragraph most equivalents leave out.

As a cross-check that our figures tie to yours before anything else: Table 3 estimates PWLB at £1,122.70m at a weighted 4.21% for 31 March 2026, and we hold 42 loans at £1,112.7m and a weighted 4.17% for the same date. £10m of principal and four basis points apart. That's a tie, and it means the numbers below are read from the same book you are.

The part with the sharpest edge is the refinancing profile. Table 8 sets a £240.3m new-borrowing requirement for 2026-27 — £193.4m of loans maturing plus £46.9m of CFR growth — landing into a market that has moved since your December advisor forecast. MUFG's Table 1 has the 5-year PWLB at 4.30% by September 2026 and the 50-year at 5.40%; today's certainty rates are 5.34% at the 5-year and 6.27% at the 50-year, roughly a full point higher across the curve. Paragraph 3.4's central bet is Bank Rate settling at 3.25% by the end of 2026-27; the 1-year OIS prices it at 4.11% today, still above the current 3.75% rather than below.

The monthly sector data at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is where a lot of that comes into view: July drew £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, after the thinnest May in years, so you can see whether the window is open, shallow or closing before a decision. Your own book is priced against the DMO's premature repayment curve daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, and with 40.48% of it sitting in the 40-50 year bucket (Table 6), the discount picture is one of the larger ones we hold. Only the DMO can quote for real, but our number is the same shape.

On training, four look most relevant to Lambeth. Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the £193.4m of maturities in 2026-27. Interest rate risk, for the size of the gap between the advisor forecast and where the curve has moved. MRP methodology, for the policy review flagged at paragraph 4.31. And our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the committee this kind of report goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

avoided: Any lecture on the EFS application — they've disclosed it themselves; leading with it reads as insensitive.
The £92m gap between the balance-sheet identity (£266.6m) and para 4.28's £359m internal figure. It's a different measure; raising it reads as a correction.
The Homes for Lambeth position — in the note but not in the email; the review is running and a cold email is the wrong channel.

Break-cost totals — our indicative net discount is very large (£177m) on a low-coupon long-dated book; the paragraph 4.21 line that rescheduling is unviable is theirs to defend and I don't want to prompt an argument.

internal_notes: Balance sheet identity ties exactly to Table 5's £266.638m under-borrowing. Paragraph 4.28's £359m internal figure uses a different measure (nets PFI and accrued MRP off the CFR base per para 4.22). £92m gap between the two — recorded here, not raised in the email.
Loan book reconciliation at 31/3/2026 ties. At 31/12/2025 our file returns 20 loans / £388.7m against their £1,071.9m — the known price_book.py Start-field artefact, per EMAIL_TEMPLATE.md.
Lambeth is in the EFS regime. Not naming that in the email but relevant context for anyone re-reading the note.

Indicative break-cost total £177.4m net discount (15.9% of principal) — unusually large because 40.48% of the book sits in the 40-50 year bucket, mostly drawn 2020-2021 at 1.87%-2.77%. The paper (para 4.21) says rescheduling is unviable because of new-borrowing rates; that argument holds even where discounts are available. Break-cost angle left out of the email.
